ox: Incorrect. Positron emission is for nuclides with too FEW neutrons (below the band). It turns a proton into a neutron.
Incorrect. Electron capture also fixes too FEW neutrons (proton-rich nuclides) by turning a proton into a neutron.
Correct. Too many neutrons for the protons means above the band of stability. β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton (n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino), lowering the neutron-to-proton ratio.
Incorrect. Gamma emission releases energy from an excited nucleus but does not change the numbers of protons or neutrons, so it cannot fix a neutron excess.

concept.t: Decay modes and the band of stability
p: Stable nuclei sit along a 'band of stability'. Nuclides above the band have too many neutrons and fix this by β⁻ decay (neutron → proton). Nuclides below the band have too few neutrons and use β⁺ decay or electron capture (proton → neutron). Very heavy nuclei (Z > 83) often emit alpha particles.

x4E_014.trap: Choosing positron emission because it sounds like it 'adds' protons. Positron emission REMOVES a proton.
x4E_014.eli: A team with too many players on one side shifts one player to the other side. The nucleus turns a neutron into a proton.
mem: Too many neutrons (above the band) → β⁻: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino.
Too few neutrons (below the band) → β⁺ or electron capture: p → n.
x4E_014.sc: Too many N → turn an N into a P → β⁻ (the electron leaves, the nucleus gains a proton).
x4E_014.mn: Neutron-rich → Negative beta. Proton-rich → Positive beta (or EC).

ox: Incorrect. The heavy daughter nucleus carries away very little of the energy because it is so much heavier than the electron. Recoil alone cannot explain a full continuous range of electron energies; the missing particle is the antineutrino.
Incorrect. Electrons do not lose varying energy in the electron cloud; they leave the atom essentially unimpeded and are detected with a continuous spread.
Incorrect. Identical nuclei of one nuclide release the SAME total decay energy every time. If it varied from nucleus to nucleus, the spread would not match the observed shape.

Correct. In β⁻ decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄) the total energy is fixed, but it is shared randomly between the electron and the antineutrino. The electron can therefore carry anything from nearly 0 up to the full amount, giving a continuous spectrum.

p: Alpha particles and gamma photons come in fixed energies because those decays have only two bodies sharing the energy. Beta decay has THREE bodies (daughter nucleus, electron and antineutrino), so the energy split can vary. The antineutrino was first proposed to rescue energy conservation in this exact observation.

x4E_028.trap: Blaming the nucleus for different energies; identical nuclei release the same total energy.
x4E_028.eli: Two kids share a fixed bag of 10 candies; one can get any number from 0 to 10, as long as the two shares add to 10.
mem: Energy is shared randomly between e⁻ and ν̄, so the electron energy is continuous.
Alpha and gamma have discrete energies; beta has a spread up to a maximum.
x4E_028.sc: Single fixed energies = two-body decay. A spread of energies = three-body decay.
x4E_028.mn: Alpha and gamma are Always-the-same; beta is Broad.

ox: Incorrect. 500 nm would mean the second photon has the same energy as the absorbed one. That would send out twice as much energy as came in.
Correct. Energy ∝ 1/λ. In units of 1/1000 nm: absorbed 500 nm = 2, first emitted 1000 nm = 1. Two in, one out, so the other must be 1 → λ = 1000 nm.
Incorrect. 1500 nm adds the wavelengths (500 + 1000). Wavelengths do not add; ENERGIES do, and energy goes as 1/λ.
Incorrect. 333 nm comes from adding the energies of the 500 and 1000 nm photons (2 + 1 = 3) instead of subtracting the emitted one from the absorbed one.

p: A photon's energy is E = hc/λ, so energy is proportional to 1/λ. When an atom absorbs a photon and relaxes in two steps, the total energy emitted equals the energy absorbed. So: 1/λ(absorbed) = 1/λ₁ + 1/λ₂.

x4E_064.eli: Think of 1/λ as 'energy coins'. A 500 nm photon is worth 2 coins and a 1000 nm photon is worth 1 coin. Two coins in, one coin out, so the other must be worth 1 coin.
mem: E = hc/λ: shorter wavelength = more energy.
Energy is conserved: energy in = sum of energies out.

fm.f: E = h·c / λ, so E ∝ 1/λ, where E = photon energy, h = Planck's constant, c = speed of light, λ = wavelength
fm.v: Use units of 1/1000 nm: absorbed (500 nm) = 2; first emitted (1000 nm) = 1; second emitted = x
fm.why: We use 1/λ because photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, and energy is what is conserved.

x4E_064.sc: Count coins in 1/1000 units: 500 nm = 2, 1000 nm = 1.
x4E_064.mn: Short = Strong: a shorter wavelength carries more energy.
